title: Nothing goes out until I say so
summary: The assistants can draft all day. Sending, posting, and spending are a different job.
body: The useful part of a bot is the draft. The send button is the part that can embarrass you.

Each one on my bench has a single job. A chief-of-staff assistant moves work between them: sales drafts, edits, research, code, the inbox, the calendar, notes. Anything that would send, post, or spend waits until I say yes.
When an assistant needs a decision, it lands on one list. I'd rather see a gap than a guess. If the source is missing or stale, it stops.
I wrote the longer version, with the drawings, on j0sh.wtf.

title: A TV that doesn't want a click
summary: Three columns on the television by the desk. No chatbot, no database, nothing to tap.
body: The TV sits across the shop. It should answer a glance, not ask me to log in.
Three columns: personal, the business, and the build. It shows what I already keep. No chatbot, no database, nothing to click.
It's open source. The useful part was what I left out.

title: Spreadsheets for people who run the place
summary: Plate cost, bakery pricing, and what the food cost did this week.
body: The owners I teach rarely need a new app first. They need a number they trust: what a plate costs, what the bakery item should sell for, whether food cost drifted this week.
OwnerMathSheets is those three sheets, in Excel and Google Sheets. If a formula can't be read out loud, it doesn't stay.
Still launching. I made it for people who run a kitchen.

title: The hub is hand-written
summary: j0sh.wtf is HTML, a Workers deploy, and no framework. The case studies live there.
body: j0sh.wtf is the hub. Hand-written HTML, Cloudflare Workers, no framework. This site is the shop. That one holds the tool notes and the case studies.
I kept it static on purpose. On Oct 27, 2026, Lighthouse on a phone scored 100 for performance, accessibility, best practices, and SEO.
The full bot-team story, with the drawings, lives on j0sh.wtf.
